## Interbranch Representation 

- Constituency service/casework
  - residents 
  - nonprofits, businesses, local governments 
  - identity groups
- Policy work 
  - oversight 
  - advising agencies

$\approx$ all substantive representation to another branch

<!--- Ellie (9/1): I'm commenting out the all representation not through legislation. I think that gets us in trouble with the speech as representation folks. No need to pick that battle. Need to cut space anyway. 
. . . 

For Congress, $\approx$ all representation not through legislation ---> 

::: {.notes}
I'm Devin Judge-Lord, presenting work with Ellie Powell and Rochelle Snyder.
As I will get into in a minute, we are building on work that has studied interbranch representation -- 
Kenny Lowande, Molly Ritchie, & Erinn Lauterbach, and the Department of Justice, both use these exact words to describe somewhat narrower subsets of what we consider interbranch representation. 
So, I just want to flag that we are positing this as a more capacious concept that we think well describes a wide range of ways that legislator offices interact with agencies.

So this is a paper about legislator offices, especially, as you will see, offices of powerhouse legislators like Robert Byrd's, whose office is in the background here. 

[Read slide] 
:::


## Interbranch Representation 

1. Who is represented (e.g., individuals, businesses, nonprofits, local governments, donors)?
2. What kind of work (e.g., casework, policy work)?

::: {.notes}
Zooming out, we can think about representation varying along two dimensions: (1) WHO someone is representing and (2) WHAT kind of action is the representative taking to do so. 

[Read slide] 
:::


## Unequal representation 

```{r}
#| label: fig-percent
#| fig-cap: "Observed levels of interbranch representation per legislator per year"
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "Senate"
#|   - "House"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| out-width: 100%

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", type, "percentile-1.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", type, "percentile-2.png"))
```

::: {.notes}
This matters because there is huge inequality in interbranch representation.

Here we have the average number of requests each legislator makes to federal agencies on the y-axis and organized by their percentile in the distribution in their chamber. 

 The top decile in both the Senate and House is doing 5 x the amount that the median legislator does. And 10 x the lower quartile.

You've probably heard of Gini Coefficients as a measure of inequality being used to describe income inequality. 
Top 10 most unequal countries, including Honduras at .47 and Zimbabwe at .50

AND THIS IS TRUE FOR ALL OF THE TYPES OF REPRESENTATION WE LOOK AT

So this is what we want to explain---how we are doing this. 
:::

::: {.notes}
The story we are telling is not just about legislators, but CONGRESSIONAL OFFICES and what they are organized to do --- they are not the same. We often study legislators as politicians, but we think it is important to also study congressional offices as bureaucracies. 

Senator Byrd's office here on the right looks like a place where you might write some letters on letterhead
Senator Cruz office looks more like a pod casting studio. His style of representation is not what some call the workhorse style. 

And indeed, Byrd is at the top of that graph I just showed you and
Cruz is at the very bottom

:::


## What we know {.smaller}

Members of Congress contact agencies to represent: 

- constituents' needs [@Fiorina1977; @Fenno1978; @MillsKalafHughes2015; @PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023; @SnyderJudgeLordPowellGrimmer2025]
- constituents' policy preferences [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023]
- shared identity groups [@LowandeRitchieLauterbach2019]
- corporate donors [@PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023]
<!-- the institution of congress [@USDepartmentofJustice2016] -->

This varies by 

- institutional position [@Lowande2018APSR; @LowandePotter2021; @LauterbachRitchie2025; @JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026]
- experience [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023; @Lowande2018APSR; @JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026] & effectiveness [@KalafHughes2023]
- party status [@Lowande2019; @Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023; @LauterbachRitchie2025]
- partisan/ideological alignment [@Lowande2019; @PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023; @Lowande2018APSR;  @LauterbachRitchie2025]

Maybe also electoral competition [@Fiorina1977; @Rivers1989; @King1991], but maybe not [@Ritchie2023]

::: {.notes}
When we started this project, it was old work by Fenno and Fiorina, and a cool new paper that Russ Mills and Nicky Kalaf-Hughes presented 10 years ago at MPSA. Since then, we've learned a number of things. 
To sum up all of this very briefly
[READ SLIDE VERY FAST]
So we have good evidence that all of these factors (except elections) matter on the margins. 
This paper aims to build on and scaffold around this work. 
:::

## What we don't know  {.smaller}

Existing studies typically: 

- Examine **one or a small number of agencies**. What does it look like across all agencies? 
- Focus on a **single type of interbranch representation**. What is the broader picture? 
- Provide lots of explanations, but less clear how it all fits together


::: {.notes}
This paper aims to build on and scaffold around this work. 

We fill in some gaps, [READ SLIDE]
:::

## A unified framework


```{r}
#| label: fig-causal
#| fig-cap: "Constituent demand, capacity, and strategic incentives"
#| out-width: "100%"
#| 
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "mermaid-figure-1.png"))
```


::: {.notes}
We organize explanations into three broad possible causes of variation that likely drive different kinds of representation. Then we ask big-pictured questions about how important each cause is in aggregate for different outcomes.
:::


## A unified framework

Demand

- more `constituents`, more `needy` or `demanding` constituents

Capacity

- more `staff`, `expertise`, etc. 

Strategic incentives to do more in a certain context

- `Reelection`, `Partisan/ideological`, `Institutional` incentives

<!--also reflect **distribution** of interests--> 

::: {.notes}
This 3-part organization is similar to how Ritchie has organized these causes, 
except perhaps that we put oversight more in the "strategic incentives" bucket, as Lowande's 2018 paper does.
Though it is probably both, the fact that we see members paying special attention to agencies in advance of joining that agency's oversight committee makes us think that Strategic Incentives is a relatively better interpretation of the oversight committee's effects.  
[READ SLIDE]


In this paper, we try to put almost all of these together. We have not yet incorporated measures of having more demanding (for example, higher-income) constituents.

We are also not focusing on predictors of allocation across agencies. That was the topic of our last year's MPSA papers. 

In this paper, we ask how much each of these factors drives inequality in how much interbranch representation different districts receive. 
:::


## Data & Design  {.smaller}

~400,000 legislator-agency-year counts (840,000 requests to 100+ agencies, 2000-2024, 430+ FOIA requests) 

. . . 

District demographics [@tidycensus], committee positions & jurisdiction [@LewisSelin2012], staff allocation [@CrossonFurnasLapiraBurgat2021] electoral competitiveness [@Thomsen2023], legislator ideology [@dwnominate2024], perceived agency ideology [@RichardsonClintonLewis2018]


::: {.notes}
We now have data from over 100 agencies from 2000-2024, including all departments except for the Department of State. It has now been 9 years since I filed that request. To be fair, State originally told us it would take 6 years, so they are only 3 years behind scheduled. 

This has taken a ton of work, negotiation, threatening lawsuits, and data cleaning, which I will not go into for the sake of time. 

We tally up the number of requests per legislator, per agency, per year, 
yielding legislator-agency-year observations

These are counts, so fit a negative binomial count model, with indicators for 
demand, like the number of people in the state  
capacity, like committee chair positions and years in office, and 
Strategic Incentives, like oversight committee membership, majority party status, whether you have a copartisan presidential electoral vulnerability, and 
ideological distance from the agency, which we get by subtracting nominee scores from Richardson-Clinton-Lewis scores. 
and other things
Errors are clustered at the legislator level. 
:::

. . . 




$$ 
\small
\begin{aligned}
Y_{ijt}\mid X_{ijt},\delta_{jt}, \gamma_{ij}  
 & \sim \text{NegBin}(\mu_{ijt},\alpha), \\
\log(\mu_{ijt}) = 
 & \beta_1 \text{District Population}_{it} + \beta_2 \text{Experience in Office}_{it}+ \\
 & \beta_3 \text{Committee Leadership Position}_{it} + \beta_4 \text{Oversight Committee Position}_{ijt}+ \\
 & \beta_5 \text{Majority Party}_{it} + \beta_6 \text{President's Party}_{it} + \\
 & \beta_7 \text{Competitive General Election}_{it} + \beta_8 \text{Competitive Primary Election}_{it} + \\
 & \beta_9 \text{Perceived Ideological Distance from Agency}_{ijt} + \\
 & ... + \delta_{jt} + \gamma_{ij} \\
 & \text{Errors clustered at the legislator level.}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-diff1}




## Design {.not-scrollable}


$Y_{ijt}$ = requests legislator $i$ makes to agency $j$ in year $t$

. . . 

$\delta_{jt}$ is an **agency--year** fixed effect

. . . 

$\gamma_{ij}$ **legislator--agency** fixed effect

- time-invariant legislator characteristics
- legislator--agency factors, including stable state or district attributes (population, demographics, local industries) that shape demand.

::: {.notes}
Important here are
fixed effects for agency-year pairs, which cover shocks to agencies like scandals and censoring in our data 
in all models 
We also estimate difference-in-differences with fixed effects for the legislator-agency pair, so those models are just about within-legislator variation over time. 

I'm happy to click over to the regression table slides in Q&A, but 
We have a large sample, so we get to focus on the magnitude of effects. 
:::

# Results

## Demand: `more constituents`

more of everything

```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-population

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-population-1.png"))

```

::: {.notes}
So I'm going to show you a bunch of average marginal effects, in percentage terms. 

The average percentage difference in legislator requests per year is on the Y-axis.

This first compares a one SD change in state population and, by implication, equal staff budgets for Senators. 

Each point estimate is the percentage change a different type of interbranch representation 

Population thus represents both demand and capacity and explains a large share of variation in the Senate, but not all of it, about 20% of the overall inequality in interbranch representation in the Senate. 


:::

## Institutional Incentives 

`Oversight positions` reflect and extend interests.

```{r}
#| label: fig-institutional
##| fig-cap: "Differences by Committee Jurisdiction"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-oversight-1.png"))
```

::: {.notes}
There is a causal effect of joining a committee, but it is smaller than the cross-sectional effect. One interpretation here is that members have preexisting interests that lead them to join committees with jurisdiction over those agencies. (e.g., I'm from ag-heavy state, I join the Ag committee), but then they do more --- the within legislator design shows members increasing policy work with an agency when they join a committee overseeing that agency. 
:::

```{r}
#| label: results-matrix
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 7.5
#| out-width: "100%"

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

type_levels <- c("Constituency\\nService", "Corporate\\nService",
                 "NGO/Gov't\\nService", "Corporate\\nPolicy",
                 "General\\nPolicy", "Total")

element_levels <- c("Demand", "Capacity", "Strategic incentives")

sub_elements <- tribble(
  ~element,               ~sub,
  "Demand",               "Number of constituents",
  "Demand",               "Neediness of constituents",
  "Demand",               "Political savvy of constituents",
  "Capacity",             "Senate",
  "Capacity",             "Experience in Congress",
  "Capacity",             "Experience in state leg.",
  "Capacity",             "Committee leadership",
  "Capacity",             "Reporting committee seat",
  "Capacity",             "Staff volume",
  "Capacity",             "Staff allocation",
  "Strategic incentives", "Partisan alignment",
  "Strategic incentives", "Ideological alignment",
  "Strategic incentives", "Business",
  "Strategic incentives", "Electoral incentives",
  "Strategic incentives", "Institutional incentives"
)

library(readr)
results <- read_csv(here::here("tables/sub_elements.csv") ) |> group_by(element, sub) |> 
  select(-`...1`) |> 
  pivot_longer(#!element, !sub,
    #cols = c(element, sub),
               cols = c(
    "Constituency\\nService",
    "NGO/Gov't\\nService",
    "General\\nPolicy",
    "Corporate\\nPolicy",
    "Total"),
    names_to = "outcome",
    values_to = "support")
# Build the full grid, then fill in your actual codings.
# Placeholder: everything set to "None" — replace with your results.
# results <- sub_elements |>
#   crossing(outcome = type_levels) |>
#   mutate(support = "None")   # <-- replace via edits below or join your own data

# # Example of hand-coding a few cells (repeat/replace as needed):
# results <- results |>
#   mutate(support = case_when(
#     sub == "Number of constituents" & outcome == "Constituency\nService" ~ "Strong",
#     sub == "Senate" & outcome == "Total" ~ "Mixed",
#     TRUE ~ support
#   ))

results2 <- results |>
  mutate(
    #outcome = gsub("\\n", "\n", outcome, fixed = TRUE),
    element = factor(element, levels = element_levels),
    sub     = factor(sub, levels = rev(sub_elements$sub)),
    outcome = factor(outcome, levels = type_levels),
    support = factor(support, levels = c("Strong", "Mixed", "None"))
  )

ggplot(results2, aes(x = outcome, y = sub)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 5.5, xmax = 6.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey92", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = support), shape = 21, size = 6, stroke = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    Strong = "#1D9E75",
    Mixed  = "#F5C518",
    None   = "white"
  )) +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  facet_grid(element ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       caption = "Strong = expected direction, significant across most measures;\nMixed = significant in some measures; None = no support.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x.top = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, lineheight = 0.9),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    strip.placement = "outside",
    strip.text.y.left = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12, angle = 0, hjust = 1),
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.y = unit(0.8, "lines"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40", hjust = 0)
  )
```



## To sum up: 

**Demand** matters

**Capacity**: Experience & staff matter; committee staff increase policy work (even for non-chairs)

Some **strategic incentives** affect some types of representation

- Little relationship with **electoral** incentives 
- Strong **partisan/ideological patterns**; mostly working with executive-branch allies
- Committee work extends preexisting interests

## Partisan/Ideological Incentives: 

`Copartisan presidents`  incentivize helping nonprofit & local government get grants and industrial policy.

```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-presidents_party
##| fig-cap: "Differences by President's Partisanship"
##| out-width: "100%"

```

::: {.notes}
In line with Berry, Burden, and Howell -- presidential pork-seeking. 
:::


::: {.notes}
When legislators are advocating for grants for nonprofits and local governments, or for public interest policy, they are mostly working with their ideological allies -- agencies perceived as being aligned with their policy agenda. 

For policy work on behalf of corporations, they are engaging with the unaligned. What's going on here is mostly comments opposing regulations, for example Republicans commenting on EPA regulations. 
:::











# Inequality in Interbranch Representation

## Why so unequal? {.incremental background-image=-"https://www.byrdcenter.org/uploads/6/7/8/7/67873389/403958_orig.jpg?592"}

Demand & capacity

- Senators representing more people with more staff 
- Unequal access to committee staff 
- Unequal experience

Strategic Incentives explain attention allocation and volume, but not inequality.

- Effects spread across high and low performers $\rightarrow$ no impact on inequality 


Implications for the effects of staffing & term limits

::: {.notes}

:::

# Tables


## Table: Staff Allocation  {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-models-staff
#| tbl-cap: "The effect of staff allocation on total requests to federal agencies"
#| out-width: 85%

load(here::here("models", type, "models_staff_spending.Rdata"))

modelsummary(models_staff_spending,
             notes = list("Robust standard errors in parentheses, clustered by legislator.",
                          "This table shows estimates of the effect of legislator capacity (chair and ranking member positions and years in office) and institutional positions that may affect strategic behavior (oversight committee membership, majority party status, co-partisan president) on levels of interbranch representation. All coefficients represent the average additional requests per year per agency; per legislator, per year effects are simply these coefficients times the number of agencies in the data.")) 
```

All coefficients represent the average additional requests per year per agency; per legislator, per year effects are simply these coefficients times the number of agencies in the data.")) 



# Effect on Inequality (Counterfactuals)


## Demand-based inequality

::: {layout="[[1,1]]"}

- more `constituents`✔️


high impact on inequality


```{r}
#| label: fig-pop-effect
#| fig-cap: "Predicted levels of interbranch representation per Senator per year"
#| out-width: 95%

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", type, "m-senate-effect-1.png"))
```

<br>
<br>
<br>
<inv>predictions</inv> compared to a `counterfactual` of equal state population
:::

::: {.notes}
So I'm going to show you a bunch of counterfactuals and compare them to predictions using the real values in the data to assess the aggregate impact. 

As with the first plot, average requests per year are on the Y-axis.
But now, the dots are predicted values for each legislator, arranged by the predicted values for our data --- the dark blue dots --- compared to predictions for those senators, with the population and budget of a senator from Wyoming. 

The first counterfactual is equal state population and, by implication, equal staff budgets for Senators. Population thus represents both demand and capacity and explains a large share of variation in the Senate, but not all of it, about 20% of the overall inequality in interbranch representation in the Senate. 
:::
